If the angular acceleration alpha is constant, then we can determine relationships that are similar in form to those for linear kinematics discussed in motion in 1D and motion in 2D and 3D. Kinematics of rotational motion. Using our intuition, we can see how the rotational quantities theta, omega, alpha and t are related to one another. We can build a set of rotational kinematic equations under a constant angular acceleration. If the angular acceleration alpha is a constant, then the average angular velocity must be a linear function with respect to time. The arithmetic angular velocity, omega bar, can be represented by omega bar equals omega zero plus omega f over 2. The time average angular velocity is given by omega bar equals change in theta over change in t, where we can solve for theta to get theta f equals theta zero plus omega bar t after having set t zero equals zero. If we know the average angular velocity omega bar of the system, then we can find the angular displacement over a given time interval. To find an equation that relates omega, alpha and t, we start with the definition of angular acceleration. Alpha equals d omega over dt. We rearrange this to get alpha dt equals d omega and then integrate both sides. Alpha integral sub t zero to the power of t dt prime equals integral sub omega zero to the power of omega f d omega. In uniform rotational motion, the angular acceleration is constant and can be pulled out of the integral. If we set t zero equals zero, then we have alpha t equals omega f minus omega zero, which we can rearrange to obtain omega f equals omega zero plus alpha t, where omega zero is the initial angular velocity. Notice how similar this equation appears compared to the linear kinematic equation with velocity. V sub f equals V sub zero plus a t. Starting with the equation, omega equals d theta over dt and rearranging to get omega dt equals d theta. We can again integrate both sides to get integral sub t zero to the power of t sub f, omega zero plus alpha t prime dt prime equals integral sub theta zero to the power of theta f d theta omega zero t plus one over two alpha t squared equals theta f minus theta zero, where we have set t zero equals zero. We can rearrange to obtain theta f equals theta zero plus omega zero times t plus one over two alpha t squared, which is a rotational counterpart to the position function of time in linear kinematics. We can find an equation that is time independent by using the linear equation for angular velocity to eliminate t, or t equals omega f minus omega zero over alpha. Change in theta equals omega zero times omega f minus omega zero over alpha plus one over two alpha times omega f minus omega zero over alpha squared. Change in theta equals omega f squared minus omega zero squared over two alpha. We can rearrange the result to obtain omega f squared equals omega zero squared plus two alpha times the change in theta. Example problem. Acceleration of a fishing reel. The problem. A deep sea fisherman hooks a big fish that swims away from the boat pulling the fishing line from his fishing reel. The whole system is initially at rest and the fishing line unwinds from the reel at a radius of 4.5 centimeters from its axis of rotation. The reel is given an angular acceleration of 110 radians per second squared for 2.0 seconds. For part A, what is the final angular velocity of the reel after two seconds? For part B, how many revolutions does the reel make? The worked solution follows. The model. The reel undergoes rotational motion about a fixed axis with constant angular acceleration. Because the angular acceleration is constant, the rotational kinematic equations for constant acceleration apply. The final angular velocity can be determined from the relationship among angular velocity, angular acceleration and time. The angular displacement can be determined from the relationship among angular displacement, angular acceleration, angular velocity and time. Once the angular displacement is found in radians, it can be converted to revolutions. The math. For part A, for rotational motion with constant angular acceleration, the final angular velocity is related to the initial angular velocity by omega f equals omega zero plus alpha t. The reel starts from rest, so the initial angular velocity is omega zero equals zero. The numerical value follows from this equation. Omega f equals zero plus 110 radians per second squared times 2.0 seconds equals 220 radians per second. For part B, for rotational motion with constant angular acceleration, the angular displacement is related to the initial angular displacement, initial angular velocity, angular acceleration and time. Theta f equals theta zero plus omega zero t plus one half alpha t squared. The reel starts from rest, so omega zero equals zero. We choose the initial angular position to be theta zero equals zero for convenience. The numerical value follows from this equation. Theta f equals zero plus zero plus one half times 110 radians per second squared times 2.0 seconds squared equals 220 rad. One revolution corresponds to two pi radians. Therefore, the number of revolutions is n equals theta f over 2 pi. The number of revolutions follows from this angular displacement, n equals 220 rad over 2 pi equals 35 rev. The conclusion. After 2.0 seconds, the reel reaches a final angular velocity of 220 radians per second. Over this same time interval, the reel rotates through 35 revolutions. This result shows that a constant angular acceleration can produce both a large angular speed and a substantial angular displacement in a short time. It also reinforces that rotational kinematics follows the same mathematical structure as linear kinematics. Example problem. Duration for a reel to stop. The problem. Now the fisherman applies a break to the spinning reel, achieving an angular acceleration of negative 300 radians per second squared. How long does it take the reel to come to a stop? The worked solution follows. The model. The reel continues to undergo rotational motion about a fixed axis, but now the angular acceleration is negative because the break reduces the angular speed. The stopping time can be determined using the constant angular acceleration kinematic relationship among angular velocity, angular acceleration, and time. Because the reel is coming to rest, the final angular velocity is zero. These ideas allow us to determine the elapsed time required for the angular velocity to decrease from its initial value to zero. The math. For rotational motion with constant angular acceleration, the final angular velocity is related to the initial angular velocity by omega f equals omega zero plus alpha t. We solve this expression for the stopping time, which gives t equals omega f minus omega zero over alpha. From the previous example, the initial angular velocity is omega zero equals 220 radians per second. The reel comes to a stop, so the final angular velocity is omega f equals zero. The stopping time follows from this expression. t equals zero minus 220 radians per second over negative 300 radians per second squared equals 0.73 seconds. The conclusion. The reel takes 0.73 seconds to come to a stop after the break is applied. This result shows that a large negative angular acceleration can reduce a substantial angular speed to zero in less than a second. It also emphasizes the importance of sine conventions in rotational kinematics, since the negative acceleration indicates that the breaking acts opposite the direction of motion. Example problem. Angular acceleration of a propeller. The problem. The angular velocity of an aircraft propeller decreases linearly from 30 radians per second to zero radians per second over a time interval of five seconds. For part A, generate a graph of the angular velocity omega as a function of time. For part B, determine the angular acceleration of the propeller from the graph. For part C, determine the angular displacement of the propeller during the five second interval. The worked solution follows. The model. The propeller rotates about a fixed axis. The angular velocity decreases linearly with time, which implies that the angular acceleration is constant. The angular acceleration is the slope of the omega versus t graph. The angular displacement can be determined in two ways. Graphically, it corresponds to the area under the angular velocity curve. Politically, it can be computed using the rotational kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration. The math. For part A, the angular velocity decreases linearly from 30 radians per second at t equals zero to zero radians per second at t equals five seconds. The resulting graph is a straight line connecting these two points. For part B, the angular acceleration equals the slope of the omega versus t graph. Alpha equals change in omega over change in t equals zero minus 30 radians per second over five seconds equals negative six radians per second squared. For part C, the angular displacement equals the area under the angular velocity curve. As the graph forms a right triangle, the area is change in theta equals one over two times base times height equals one over two times five seconds times 30 radians per second equals 75 rad. We can verify this result using the rotational kinematic equation theta f equals theta zero plus omega zero t plus one over two alpha t squared. Setting theta f equals zero and substituting the known values gives theta f equals 30 times five plus one over two times negative six times five squared equals 150 minus 75 equals 75 rad. The conclusion, the angular acceleration of the propeller is alpha equals negative six radians per second squared. During the five second interval, the propeller rotates through an angular displacement of theta equals 75 rad. This result is consistent with both the graphical interpretation of the motion and the rotational kinematic equations.
